newsitem.title: USA: U.S. West spot power up amid cool weather, outages.
newsitem.headline: U.S. West spot power up amid cool weather, outages.

text.p: Western U.S. spot power prices ended higher amid unplanned unit outages and a return to seasonally cool temperatures, market sources said Tuesday.
"Prices started up, but then tailed off," said one northern California trader.
He said many market players learned only after the close of daily trading Monday that Pacific Gas and Electric Co's 1,200 megawatt (MW) Helms hydropower plant was idled by a fire on Saturday.
That news boosted buying interest early Tuesday, but the uptrend failed to hold, the trader said.
A PG&E spokesman told Reuters early Monday that unit could be out of service for as long as two weeks.
In addition, restart of the 790 MW unit 1 at the Mohave coal-fired plant in Nevada has been pushed back to Wednesday, a spokesman for Southern California Edison Co said Tuesday.
The Mohave unit was taken off-line Friday due to a tube leak, but work is still underway on a generator, he said.
Restart of a 750 MW unit at the Navajo coal-fired plant in Arizona was also said to be delayed to Wednesday, after an unplanned outage began Friday.
Temperatures throughout the West were described as within a degree or two of normal.
Wednesday firm, peak electricity at the California-Oregon border (COB) was quoted at $11.50-12.50 per megawatt hour (MWh), compared with $11.00-12.00 for Monday.
Firm, peak power at Mid-Columbia (Mid-C) was at $10.00-11.50, while off-peak was at $5.00-7.00.
Firm, peak Palo Verde (PV) electricity was at $13.00-$13.75, while off-peak was quoted at $6.50-8.00.
Next-day firm, peak power at Four Corners was quoted at $13.00-14.00, while off-peak was at $7.00-8.00.
